overall_summary: FACTVERSE's audience shows a clear preference for extreme cosmic anomalies, planetary physics paradoxes, and mind-bending space-time comparisons. Standard psychology facts and basic animal trivia consistently underperform, indicating that the channel's growth engine lies in high-concept, visually dramatic space and physics content.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice Will Break Your Brain!' reached 1,055 views, 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' reached 1,023 views, and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' hit 721 views.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme planetary conditions, focusing on sensory-rich, highly visual concepts (e.g., iron rain, diamond oceans, extreme gravity) with dramatic, curiosity-inducing titles.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' achieved 302 views, 'Sharks Are OLDER Than Saturn's Rings?' reached 274 views, and 'Why Your Head Is Older Than Your Feet' hit 264 views.
winning_patterns.action: Create a recurring sub-series of 'Time Paradox' shorts that contrast human perception of history and physics against cosmic reality.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' struggled across multiple uploads, peaking at only 53 views, while 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' got only 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Phase out standard psychological advice and brain hacks unless they can be framed with a massive evolutionary or sci-fi twist.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Octopuses Have THREE Hearts' peaked at 183 views, and 'The Only Animal That Can Live Forever' got only 69 views.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid basic biological trivia. If featuring animals, pivot to prehistoric beasts or cinematic survival stories.

next_video.concept: WASP-76b: The Planet Where It Rains Molten Iron
next_video.opening_direction: Start with a hyper-realistic visual of molten metal droplets falling onto a dark surface: 'On this planet, the evening forecast isn't rain... it's boiling iron.'
next_video.twist_direction: Explain that the daytime side is so hot it vaporizes metal, which winds then sweep to the freezing night side, causing it to condense and rain down as liquid metal.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful 'extreme planetary weather' pattern (similar to the burning ice and ruby rain videos) while maintaining a tight, high-retention 18-second duration.

experiment: Test a 'What If' scenario focusing on a cosmic threat to Earth, such as 'What If a Rogue Star Entered Our Solar System?', to see if existential space dread performs as well as exoplanet anomalies.
